steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on humanoid locomotion as next token prediction. Motivate it from language modeling with transformers, explain how we model sensorimotor trajectories (including incomplete ones like human videos), and summarize the real-world and simulation results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Large transformers trained by next-word prediction on Internet language data
2. Can the same kind of modeling learn sensory and motor representations?
3. Our approach: humanoid control as modeling sensorimotor trajectories with a causal transformer
4. Benefits, and learning from incomplete trajectories such as human videos
5. Validation on real-world humanoid locomotion and main findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Language modeling background
- last decade of AI: large neural nets trained on diverse Internet data -> impressive results across settings
- core enablers: large transformer models, generative modeling of massive language data from the Internet
- next-word prediction -> rich representations; transfer to downstream tasks, multi-task learning, few-shot learning

2. Beyond language?
- exclusive to language? sensory and motor representations in a similar fashion?
- vision: autoregressive modeling, related masked modeling approaches
- sensorimotor representations: positive signal in manipulation, but area largely unexplored

3. Our approach
- humanoid control = data modeling of large collections of sensorimotor trajectories
- like language: general transformer, autoregressively predict shifted input sequences
- unlike language: robotics data high-dimensional, multiple input modalities
- modalities: sensors (joint encoders, inertial measurement units) + motor commands
- sensorimotor trajectories = "sentences of the physical world"
- tokenize trajectories, causal transformer predicts shifted tokens
- predict complete sequences (sensory + motor tokens): joint data distribution, not conditional action distribution

4. Benefits + incomplete data
- predict more bits -> richer model of the world
- can use noisy / imperfect trajectories with suboptimal actions
- generalizes to trajectories with missing information
- core observation: incomplete trajectory -> predict what is present, replace missing tokens with learnable mask tokens
- intuition: good predictions without full information -> better model of physical world
- human videos from the Internet: see movement, no motor commands or complete sensory inputs; method learns from them effectively

5. Validation
- real-world humanoid locomotion; full-sized Digit humanoid (Agility Robotics)
- dataset collected in simulation: complete trajectories from RL-trained neural network policy
- incomplete trajectories, three sources: (i) Agility Robotics MPC controller, (ii) human motion capture, (iii) YouTube videos of humans
- videos reconstructed with computer vision; mocap + YouTube retargeted via inverse kinematics
- transformer trained to autoregressively predict trajectories; test time: execute actions autoregressively, ignore sensory predictions
- zero-shot real-world deployment, different surfaces; locations in San Francisco over one week; Figure 1, project page videos
- extensive simulation study: offline-only autoregressive policies comparable to state-of-the-art RL in tested settings
- benefits from incomplete trajectories, favorable scaling
- conclusion: promising path for real-world robot control via generative modeling of sensorimotor trajectories

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Over the last decade, AI has shown that big neural networks trained on diverse data from the Internet can give impressive results in many different settings. The main thing behind this wave of AI has been large transformer models that are trained by generative modeling of huge amounts of language data from the Internet. By predicting the next word, these models learn rich representations of language, and these can be transferred to downstream tasks, used for multi-task learning, and used to learn in a few-shot manner.

Is this kind of modeling only for language? Could we learn strong models of sensory and motor representations in the same way? We have in fact seen that good representations of high-dimensional visual data can be learned by autoregressive modeling and by related masked modeling approaches. There has also been some positive signal on learning sensorimotor representations for manipulation, but this area is still mostly unexplored.

In this paper we treat humanoid control as data modeling of large collections of sensorimotor trajectories. As in language, we train a general transformer model to autoregressively predict shifted input sequences. But the data in robotics is different from language. It is high-dimensional and it has multiple input modalities, which include sensors, like joint encoders or inertial measurement units, and also motor commands. Together these give sensorimotor trajectories, and we view them as the sentences of the physical world. Seeing it this way suggests a simple instantiation of the language modeling framework for robotics: we tokenize the input trajectories and train a causal transformer model to predict shifted tokens. An important point is that we predict the complete input sequences, with both sensory and motor tokens. So we are modeling the joint data distribution and not the conditional action distribution.

There are several benefits to this. First, the neural network is trained to predict more bits of information, so it gets a richer model of the world. Second, we can use noisy or imperfect trajectories that may have suboptimal actions. Third, the framework can be generalized to learning from trajectories where some information is missing.

5. Learning from incomplete trajectories
- incomplete trajectory (missing sensory or motor info): predict what is present, learnable mask tokens for missing tokens
- intuition: good predictions without full information -> better model of physical world
- human videos from the Internet: movement visible, no motor commands / complete sensory inputs; we learn from them effectively

6. Validation setup
- real-world humanoid locomotion, full-sized Digit humanoid (Agility Robotics)
- simulation dataset: complete trajectories from RL policy; incomplete from (i) Agility Robotics MPC controller, (ii) human mocap, (iii) YouTube videos of humans
- computer vision to reconstruct videos; inverse kinematics retargeting
- train transformer autoregressively; test time execute actions, ignore sensory predictions

7. Results
- zero-shot real-world deployment, different surfaces, San Francisco, one week; Figure 1, project page
- simulation study: comparable to state-of-the-art RL; benefits from incomplete trajectories; favorable scaling

8. Closing: promising path via generative modeling of sensorimotor trajectories

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Over the last decade, AI has shown that big neural networks trained on diverse data from the Internet can give impressive results in many different settings. The main thing behind this wave of AI has been large transformer models that are trained by generative modeling of huge amounts of language data from the Internet. By predicting the next word, these models learn rich representations of language, and these can be transferred to downstream tasks, used for multi-task learning, and used to learn in a few-shot manner.

Is this kind of modeling only for language? Could we learn strong models of sensory and motor representations in the same way? We have in fact seen that good representations of high-dimensional visual data can be learned by autoregressive modeling and by related masked modeling approaches. There has also been some positive signal on learning sensorimotor representations for manipulation, but this area is still mostly unexplored.

In this paper we treat humanoid control as data modeling of large collections of sensorimotor trajectories. As in language, we train a general transformer model to autoregressively predict shifted input sequences. But the data in robotics is different from language. It is high-dimensional and it has multiple input modalities, which include sensors, like joint encoders or inertial measurement units, and also motor commands. Together these give sensorimotor trajectories, and we view them as the sentences of the physical world. Seeing it this way suggests a simple instantiation of the language modeling framework for robotics: we tokenize the input trajectories and train a causal transformer model to predict shifted tokens. An important point is that we predict the complete input sequences, with both sensory and motor tokens. So we are modeling the joint data distribution and not the conditional action distribution.

There are several benefits to this. First, the neural network is trained to predict more bits of information, so it gets a richer model of the world. Second, we can use noisy or imperfect trajectories that may have suboptimal actions. Third, the framework can be generalized to learning from trajectories where some information is missing.

The core observation is that if a trajectory is incomplete, meaning some of the sensory or motor information is missing, we can still learn from it by predicting whatever information is there and replacing the missing tokens with learnable mask tokens. The intuition is that a model that has learned to make good predictions even when information is absent will have a better model of the physical world. Human videos from the Internet are a very important source of this kind of data. In videos we can see human movement, but we do not have the motor commands or the complete sensory inputs. We show that our method can learn from such data effectively.

To validate the method we apply it to real-world humanoid locomotion, which is a challenging task. We use the Digit robot, a full-sized humanoid developed by Agility Robotics. First we collect a dataset of sensorimotor trajectories in simulation. It has complete trajectories from a neural network policy trained with reinforcement learning, and also incomplete trajectories that come from three different sources: (i) the Agility Robotics controller, which is based on model predictive control, (ii) motion capture of humans, and (iii) YouTube videos of humans. The human videos are reconstructed with computer vision techniques, and both the motion capture and the YouTube trajectories are retargeted with inverse kinematics. Then we train a transformer model to autoregressively predict the trajectories. At test time we execute the actions autoregressively and we ignore the sensory predictions.

We show that the policy can be deployed in the real world zero-shot and that it walks on different surfaces. We deployed the model in a range of different locations in San Francisco over one week. Figure 1 has examples, and videos are on our project page. To evaluate different aspects of the approach quantitatively, we do an extensive study in simulation. We find that our autoregressive policies, trained only from offline data, are comparable to state-of-the-art approaches that use reinforcement learning in the settings we tested. We also find that the approach can easily benefit from incomplete trajectories and that it has favorable scaling properties.

These results suggest a promising path toward learning challenging real-world robot control tasks through generative modeling of large collections of sensorimotor trajectories.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The last decade of artificial intelligence (AI) has shown that large neural networks trained on diverse datasets from the Internet can lead to impressive results across many settings. The core enablers of this wave of AI have been large transformer models [1] trained by generative modeling of massive quantities of language data from the Internet [2,3,4,5,6]. By predicting the next word, these models acquire rich representations of language that can be transferred to downstream tasks [2], used for multi-task learning [4,5], and used to learn in a few-shot manner [6].

Are such modeling techniques exclusive to language? Can we learn powerful models of sensory and motor representations in a similar way? Indeed, we have seen that good representations of high-dimensional visual data can be learned by autoregressive modeling [7] and related masked modeling approaches [8]. While there has been positive signal on learning sensorimotor representations in the context of manipulation [9], this area remains largely unexplored.

In this paper, we cast humanoid control as data modeling of large collections of sensorimotor trajectories. As in language, we train a general transformer model to autoregressively predict shifted input sequences. In contrast to language, however, the nature of data in robotics is different: it is high-dimensional and contains multiple input modalities. These modalities include sensors, like joint encoders or inertial measurement units, as well as motor commands, and together they give rise to sensorimotor trajectories, which we view as the sentences of the physical world. This perspective suggests a simple instantiation of the language modeling framework in the robotic context. We tokenize the input trajectories and train a causal transformer model to predict shifted tokens. Importantly, we predict complete input sequences, including both sensory and motor tokens. In other words, we model the joint data distribution rather than the conditional action distribution.

This has several benefits. First, the neural network is trained to predict more bits of information and therefore acquires a richer model of the world. Second, we can leverage noisy or imperfect trajectories that may contain suboptimal actions. Third, our framework can be generalized to learning from trajectories with missing information.

Our core observation is that if a trajectory is incomplete, i.e., some of the sensory or motor information is missing, we can still learn from it by predicting whatever information is present and replacing the missing tokens with learnable mask tokens. The intuition is that if the model has learned to make good predictions even in the absence of information, it will have acquired a better model of the physical world. Human videos from the Internet are a very important source of such data: we can observe human movement in videos, but we do not get access to the motor commands or complete sensory inputs. We demonstrate that our method can learn from such data sources effectively.

To validate our method, we apply it to the challenging task of real-world humanoid locomotion, using the full-sized Digit humanoid robot developed by Agility Robotics. We first collect a dataset of sensorimotor trajectories in simulation. These include complete trajectories from a neural network policy trained with reinforcement learning [10], as well as incomplete trajectories from three different sources: (i) the Agility Robotics controller based on model predictive control, (ii) motion capture of humans, and (iii) YouTube videos of humans. We reconstruct human videos using computer vision techniques and retarget both motion capture and YouTube trajectories via inverse kinematics. We then train a transformer model to autoregressively predict trajectories. At test time, we execute the actions autoregressively and ignore the sensory predictions.

We demonstrate that our policy can be deployed in the real world zero-shot and walk on different surfaces. Specifically, we deploy our model across a range of different locations in San Francisco over the course of one week. See Figure 1 for examples and our project page for videos. To quantitatively evaluate different aspects of our approach, we perform an extensive study in simulation. We find that our autoregressive policies trained from offline data alone are comparable to state-of-the-art approaches that use reinforcement learning [10] in the tested settings. We further find that our approach readily benefits from incomplete trajectories and has favorable scaling properties.

These findings suggest a promising path toward learning challenging real-world robot control tasks by generative modeling of large collections of sensorimotor trajectories.
